Zelda II. The red-headed step-child of the series.

It's tough. You must know that going in. There is no help system. You have to talk to villagers to get information. All of them. Some of them are Ganon's spies and will turn in to enemies right in front of you, so you have to be careful. You will be told when there are spies around though, as long as you talk to people and read what they have to say. You have to explore of your own volition and there are no way-points to guide you. The combat is simple and beautiful. High and low guard, how and low attacks, downward stabs and upward thrusts when jumping. Some basic magic. It feels good though, parrying and blocking with the Iron Knuckles in Zelda II is fun.

The dungeons are labyrinthine, many of them with instant-death jumping pitfalls. You only get three lives before it's GAME OVER RETURN OF GANON (because they spilt Link's blood on his ashes to resurrect him, fucking metal) and then you respawn in the North Palace in front of the sleeping Princess Zelda (not the one from the first game that took place a couple of years before, the other one, the older one that was put in to a deep sleep centuries ago and the Prince/King, in his grief, declared that all daughters of the royal line will bear her name in memory of her. That's the Legend of Zelda. Get it?) You still have your items from the dungeons and whatnot though so you can easily get back to where you were via the overworld.

Zelda II cannot be taken at face value, or just by the name alone. It's not a "proper" Zelda game. It's more of a Faxanadu/Final Fantasy mash-up. If you go in to it not expecting a "proper" Zelda game (which is pretty asinine because this was only the second game and there was no "Zelda formula" at this point) you will be frustrated and disappointed. If you go in to it open-minded and expecting to have to work for it, which is actually more common now than at any point since the 16-bit era since the Souls series has renewed gaming culture's love affair with actual difficulty and hardship and triumph, I'm pretty sure you will find the diamond in the rough.

You are Gordon Freeman. You have been contracted by the mysterious man-in-the-suit, the G-Man, and places in stasis. But now... time's up. You are summoned back to the world, and given a task you don't understand and shown images of things you half-recognize.

The G-Man places you on a train arriving in City 17, the new capitol of the world. Nothing is the way it was; a derelict, barely maintained station dotted with advanced monitoring systems and security, with propaganda being broadcast by none other than your old boss. Humanoid figures in insectile masks enforce their will on the travelers. You've been gone nearly twenty years.

Immediately after the G-Man gave you the "choice" to work for him, an alien race called the Combine entered the portal you unwittingly created at the will of the mysterious man-in-the-suit. It took them four hours to conquer earth. They rule here now, with an iron fist an with no will strong enough to oppose them. The humans are oppressed and harvested to be used as slaves, and the vortigaunts -- a species that you fought as they fled from their oppressors -- are being exterminated as they are found.

But all that has changed now. The G-Man has set in motion a chain of events that can not be stopped. The one truly Free Man has returned -- the Combine's Reckoning is at hand.

Rise and shine, Mister Freeman. Rise and... shine. Not that I... wish to imply you have been sleeping on the job. No one is more deserving of a rest, and all the effort in the world would have gone to waste until... well, let's just say your hour has... come again. The right man in the wrong place can make all the difference in the world. So, wake up, Mister Freeman. Wake up and... smell the ashes...

I used to play Terraria with some gamer friend I knew back in middle school; he lives far away now. I first heard of Starbound when this guy showed me this video. I was instantly in love. As the release of Starbound beta on Steam approached, I posted on Reddit and the Starbound forums for people with a playstyle similar to mine. I was always slow to progress through the game, building and soaking up all of the atmosphere. My Terraria friend was the opposite, so I needed new people to play with.

From the threads I posted, there were several candidates. Out of the 7 or 8 of them, there were about 4 that played regularly including me. These guys were Kneesocks (Linal), Kylorian (Pat) and Aoiluna (Cody). I named us Nesano's Starbound Enjoyment Group (N-SEG) and made us a logo. Linal was the one that hosted the server that we'd all play on, so I built him this shrine out of Floran building material to show my gratitude. That's him in the shrine and I'm standing on the far right taking the screenshot.

We didn't spend as much time building and adventuring as I'd have liked, but together we explored the galaxy and built many outposts. Science labs were my thing. Although one of us was missing, I took this picture of us playing music together on the rolling hills of an unnamed planet. That's me on the right, Linal on the left and either Pat or Cody in the center. I wish I would have taken more screenshots, but I'm glad I got this one.

I just felt like sharing that story with all of you, it's one of my best multiplayer experiences because I got to experience a game that's best played multiplayer with a few other people that I ended up playing regularly with.

Back to Childhood by Demizu Posuka

You know, it's crazy how growing up and being bombarded by societies culture and expectations make you forget the imagination we had as children. Well at least for me. I remember going into the alley behind my house and building little forts and imagining being an explorer. I remember wondering past my neighborhood block into another just to explore the alleys there. Everyday was an adventure after school.

There was a little wooded area down the street from where we lived when I was a child. All the neighborhood kids would gather there. We would build our forts and play war or perhaps cowboys and indians. It was our place. Nobody bothered us and we always felt safe.

There was an abandoned underground cement structure we called the bomb shelter. More likely it was a fruit cellar or something equally less dramatic. Naturally that didn't matter to us. It became a regular part of our daily life, hiding from the world and the infamous atomic threat that all the adults seemed certain was imminent.

Thankfully, that never came to pass and now I am able to look back on those times with fond memories.
